lines.text: Viking kings and runestones, a queen of three crowns, fairy tales and plastic bricks. This is the story of Denmark.
It begins with Harald Bluetooth, the Viking king who united Denmark and brought it to Christianity.
From his reign the kingdom of Denmark took shape, on the Jutland peninsula and its many islands.
At Jelling, Harald and his father Gorm raised great runestones, still called Denmark's birth certificate.
Harald's grandson Cnut took the English crown in 1016, and ruled Denmark and Norway too, an empire around the North Sea.
Around 1070, five Viking ships were sunk to block a fjord near Roskilde. Raised again, they can be seen there today.
A small fishing village on the Sound grew into a royal city, Copenhagen, the capital.
Queen Margaret the First brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden together under one crown in the Kalmar Union.
In 1536 Denmark broke with Rome and became Lutheran, as it remains.
On an island in the Sound, Tycho Brahe built an observatory and charted the stars more precisely than anyone before the telescope.
At Helsingor, the castle of Kronborg rose to guard the Sound. Shakespeare made it Elsinore, the home of Hamlet.
Hans Christian Andersen, born in Odense in 1805, would write The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, tales of his own invention.
In Copenhagen, Soren Kierkegaard wrote of anxiety, choice and faith, and is often called the first existentialist.
In 1843 Tivoli Gardens opened its gates in the capital, one of the oldest amusement parks in the world.
Niels Bohr pictured electrons leaping between energy levels, won the Nobel Prize, and made Copenhagen a home of quantum physics.
In 1904 the shipping firm Maersk was founded. It grew into one of the largest container lines on Earth.
In 1913 Andersen's Little Mermaid took her seat on a rock in Copenhagen harbour.
Novo Nordisk began making insulin in the twenties. Later, with Ozempic, it was for a time Europe's most valuable company.
In April 1940, German troops occupied Denmark. The occupation lasted five years.
In 1943, Danes hid their Jewish neighbours and ferried nearly all of them across the Sound to safety in Sweden.
After the war, a toymaker in Billund made the first plastic Lego bricks, and children everywhere started building.
Frederik the Tenth became king in 2024, when his mother, Queen Margrethe, stepped down.
And Mette Frederiksen has led the government as prime minister since 2019.
From Viking runestones to Lego bricks, Denmark has built far more than its size would suggest.
